status_summary: The work-requirement half is law and operative: Public Law 119-21 (signed 2025-07-04) raised the SNAP time-limit age for adults without dependents to 64, narrowed the child exemption to children under 14, removed exemptions for veterans, homeless people and former foster youth, and limited area waivers, effective on enactment, with USDA guidance in September and October 2025. The same law also requires Medicaid community engagement (80 hours a month) for expansion adults, implemented by a CMS interim final rule published 2026-06-03 (effective 2026-07-31; states must comply by 2027-01-01). The marriage-penalty half is not addressed in the sources read: a coalition letter to the House Speaker on 2026-01-06 treats welfare marriage-penalty reform as a future reconciliation goal, and a July 2026 report describes a bill to remove a marriage penalty in the state and local tax deduction cap, which is a proposal, not law. The interim final rule is challenged by 23 States, the District of Columbia and the Governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania in Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. Oz (D. Mass.), where Judge Richard G. Stearns denied a preliminary injunction without prejudice on 2026-07-29 for lack of irreparable harm, so the rule remains in effect; summary judgment motions were argued on 2026-10-22 and taken under advisement. A Rhode Island temporary restraining order of 2025-10-31 against early termination of SNAP time-limit waivers ended with a stipulated dismissal in March 2026 and did not reach the statutory requirements.

timeline.event: Public Law 119-21 is signed; its SNAP section 10102 raises the able-bodied adult work requirement upper age to 64, limits the dependent exemption to children under 14, removes exemptions for veterans, homeless people and former foster youth, and limits area waivers, effective on enactment.
The same law adds section 71119, a Medicaid community engagement requirement for certain adults.
USDA issues guidance on the revised adult exemptions under the new law (ages 18 to 64, child exemption under 14, removal of veteran, homeless and former foster youth exemptions).

The U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (Rhode Island State Council of Churches v. Rollins, No. 1:25-cv-00569, Chief Judge McConnell) grants a temporary restraining order orally on 2025-10-31, written on 2025-11-01 (ECF 19); besides requiring SNAP benefit payments from contingency funds during the shutdown, paragraph 7 enjoins USDA from terminating able-bodied adults without dependents (ABAWD) waivers early on the ground that they were approved for lack of sufficient jobs.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court, D.R.I. (order, via CourtListener)

timeline.event: A coalition of conservative and faith-based groups writes to the House Speaker asking that a reconciliation package address welfare marriage penalties and phase-outs; the letter identifies no enacted change to marriage penalties in 2025 or 2026.
timeline.source: Coalition letter hosted by Rep. Grothman

timeline.event: The parties' joint stipulation of dismissal (ECF 53, filed 2026-03-02) ends Rhode Island State Council of Churches v. Rollins, and the case closes on 2026-03-03; the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse summary describes the dismissal as moot and notes that the waivers at issue expired 2026-03-01.

CMS publishes the Medicaid community engagement interim final rule (effective 2026-07-31): expansion adults ages 19 to 64 must show 80 hours a month of work, service, a work program, education or equivalent income, with listed exemptions, and states must comply by 2027-01-01.
Trade press reports a new bill that would double the state and local tax deduction cap for joint filers, described as eliminating a marriage penalty in that cap; it is a proposal and not law.

In Commonwealth of Massachusetts v. Oz (D. Mass. No. 1:26-cv-12962-RGS), brought by 23 States, the District of Columbia and the Governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania against limits in the CMS interim final rule implementing H.R. 1 (a work requirement in the definition of medically frail, a 12-month look-back for frailty claims, and a work requirement on the short-term hardship exception), Judge Richard G. Stearns issued a Memorandum and Order on Plaintiffs' Motion for a Preliminary Injunction (Document 94) denying the motion without prejudice because the States had not shown irreparable harm, noting the Government's representation that it would reimburse 90 percent of state eligibility-system costs; the court stated that the ruling reflected no view on the merits and that it would set an expedited schedule for full merits briefing before the 2027-01-01 implementation deadline.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Document 94 (RECAP copy of the filed order)

title: Eliminate marriage penalties in welfare and taxes; add work requirements for food stamps
uncertainties: The statute text of Public Law 119-21 was not read directly for this record; SNAP changes come from the USDA memo and the Medicaid section number from the c14-05 record and the CMS rule. Whether the law changed any marriage penalties inside the tax code (for example in deductions, credits or phase-outs) was not systematically examined: a limited search found only advocacy briefs, a coalition letter and one trade-press bill report, none of which show an enacted elimination, so the absence of change is an inference from limited evidence. The Foreword's phrase food stamps maps to SNAP. Related records c10-01 and c14-05 have more detail on each program. The SNAP time limit now reaches adults through age 64, per the USDA October 2025 guidance. The Rhode Island order of 2025-11-01 (ECF 19) was read on CourtListener and the docket history on the Clearinghouse; the Clearinghouse lists only temporary restraining orders, no preliminary injunction. Review of 2026-10-27: Ballotpedia News is a lead-only host and was removed as a source; its report that USDA guidance of 2026-02-26 kept the affected ABAWD waivers through their original end dates is an unverified lead, and the Clearinghouse page does not mention that guidance. The Clearinghouse summary gives the mootness ground as full reinstatement of SNAP benefits on 2025-11-12, while also noting waiver expiry on 2026-03-01; the stipulation itself was not read. The Massachusetts v. Oz order of 2026-07-29 (Document 94) was read on 2026-10-28 in a RECAP copy of the filed order, with the docket on CourtListener (last updated 2026-10-27); the order decided only the preliminary injunction motion and stated that it did not anticipate the court's views on the merits. The plaintiffs' Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (Doc. 103) and the defendants' Cross Motion for Summary Judgment (Doc. 138) were argued on 2026-10-22 and taken under advisement; when the court will rule, and whether before the 2027-01-01 implementation deadline, is not known. The suit's filing date of 2026-06-29 rests on the Clearinghouse page, not on a court document read. Sibling record c14-05 carries the same court events.
